questions.q: According to this lesson, what makes a number a governance KPI rather than just a metric someone computed once?
options: It is expressed as a percentage
It's tied to a decision, has a named owner, and is tracked consistently over time
It appears in a steering committee slide deck
questions.explain: A KPI is defined by being tied to a decision, owned, and tracked over time — not by its format or audience.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT one of the four KPI categories the lesson identifies?
questions.explain: The four categories are program health, data quality, adoption, and issue resolution. Office headcount isn't a governance KPI category.

questions.q: What is a leading indicator, per this lesson?
options: The first KPI listed on a dashboard
A metric that predicts a problem before it shows up in outcomes, like domains missing an assigned steward
A metric that only confirms what already happened
questions.explain: A leading indicator gives advance warning; a lagging indicator confirms an outcome after the fact.

questions.q: The lesson gives "number of policies published" as an example of what?
options: A vanity metric — it looks good but doesn't drive any decision
questions.explain: It goes up regardless of whether anyone follows the policies, so it fails the lesson's test: would anyone change what they do if it moved?

questions.q: Why does the lesson say a program that only reports lagging indicators is a problem?
options: Lagging indicators cost more to compute
It's always explaining the past instead of catching problems before they show up in results
questions.explain: Lagging indicators confirm outcomes after the fact; without leading indicators, a program has no early warning before a bad outcome lands.
